newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland to publish monthly consumer price data.
newsitem.headline: Ireland to publish monthly consumer price data.

text.p: Ireland will bring its inflation reporting into line with the rest of the European Union when it publishes monthly consumer price data for January on Tuesday.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) previously published the consumer price index (CPI) on a quarterly basis but is moving to monthly releases as part of an EU data harmonisation process.
Analysts say interpretation of the January figures will be difficult as there are no comparable monthly readings for 1996.
"There are no seasonally adjusted or previous CPI readings for January so the market may await the February figures before passing any judgement," Goodbody Stockbrokers said.
The new index will also incorporate updated weights based on a recently released 1994/95 household budget survey.
Analysts expect the effect of the January sales to exert downward pressure on the index while excise duties announced in the January 22 budget won't show up in the figures.
They forecast an increase of 0.1 to 0.3 percent on the fourth quarter of 1996 while the index is expected to rise by 1.7 to 1.8 percent on the first quarter of last year.
But economists say it will not be possible to calculate a proper year-on-year rate until monthly data for February 1997 is released as the first quarter reading last year was taken in mid-February.
Irish financial markets will also be keeping a close eye on the Central Bank of Ireland's annual monetary policy statement, due for publication at 1630 GMT on Tuesday.
The statement will be closely scrutinised for clues to the bank's view on inflation, interest rates and the current strength of the Irish pound in the ERM grid.
The punt has remained firmly positioned at the top of the grid for several weeks, around 11 percent above the French franc, the weakest currency.

Analysts are concerned that further sterling strength could drag it higher, possibly pushing it through its 15 percent ceiling and jeopardising Ireland's credentials for joining Economic and monetary union (EMU).

The Maastricht treaty requires that a member state "has respected the normal fluctuation margins provided for by the exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System without severe tensions for at least two years before examination".
But most analysts believe the bank is unlikely to make any clear statement on exchange or interest rates and will probably just highlight the risks to Irish inflation.
"The central bank is unlikely to offer hostages to fortune in its policy statement but it should hit the usual cautious notes on the fiscal stance and credit data," Goodbody Stockbrokers said.
